title: Al-Tusi's observatory
hookLine: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi builds an observatory at Maragha under Mongol rule

cards: On a hilltop above the town of Maragha, in Persia, workmen are laying stone for a building whose whole purpose is to watch the sky.
Inside will go great instruments for measuring where the stars and planets stand, and a library beside them. The money comes from Hulagu, the same Mongol prince whose army sacked Baghdad.
The man in charge is a Persian scholar, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. The storm that, the chroniclers say, drowned books in a river is now paying for star charts. Today: al-Tusi's observatory.

teach.b: Al-Tusi was a scholar of many fields: astronomy, mathematics, philosophy, ethics, and the theology of the Shia tradition he belonged to.
He came into Hulagu's service and persuaded the prince to build the observatory at Maragha.
They watched the sky night after night and wrote tables of where the heavens moved, tables astronomers went on using.

teach.h: THE TUSI COUPLE: CIRCLES MAKE A LINE.
teach.b: Al-Tusi also worked on a hard problem from the Greek astronomy he had inherited: how to explain the planets' motions using only circles turning evenly. His answer is now called the Tusi couple.
Picture a small circle rolling inside a bigger one, twice as wide. A point on the small circle doesn't go round and round. It goes straight back and forth, in a line.
Some historians have noticed a very similar device in Copernicus's work, much later, and still debate how it got there. So, learning survived. Not untouched, not without cost.
But the habit of looking up and measuring carefully didn't die with Baghdad. It moved to a hilltop and kept going. Why would a believer care about star tables?
Partly for prayer: the times of prayer and the direction of Mecca are worked out from the sky. And partly because the Qur'an keeps pointing up.
In surah Al 'Imran, in Pickthall's English: "Lo! In the creation of the heavens and the earth and (in) the difference of night and day are tokens (of His sovereignty) for men of understanding."
For al-Tusi's circle, measuring the sky was one way of reading those tokens.

how: Muslims use the sky to set the times of prayer, the direction of Mecca and the months of the lunar calendar, and the sighting of the new moon marks the start and end of Ramadan for communities that follow local sighting.

games.q: you're al-Tusi. your patron is the prince whose army sacked Baghdad, and he will pay for an observatory if you ask. what do you do?
games.why: he persuaded Hulagu to build it at Maragha. scholars came, the sky was measured, and learning survived.

practice: Look at the sky: step outside or go to a window, or, if you can't, close your eyes and remember the last night sky you really saw.
Don't name anything; just notice how much is up there that you didn't put there, keeping its own time.
If you pray, bring to mind the words the Qur'an gives just after that verse, our Lord, you did not create this in vain; if not, let the size of it sit with you.

wordCard.voice: Al-Tusi's observatory. Built at Maragha under Mongol rule by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, a place to measure the sky after the fall of Baghdad. Today's words.

orig.note: Arabic: an observatory, a place for watching the sky.
